newsitem.title: USA: Price funds deserve a close look.
newsitem.headline: Price funds deserve a close look.

text.p: On Oct. 31, Franklin Templeton became the official owners of Heine Securities, which Franklin agreed to buy from value investor Michael Price last July.
That means investors must now pay a sales charge of up to 4.5 percent to invest in the Mutual Series funds. Are the funds worth the load? Probably so, at least for long-term investors.

During the past decade, Price, 44, has cemented his reputation as one of the great value investors of his generation. His flagship fund, Mutual Shares (800-448-3863; $1,000 minimum investment; 4.5 percent load), has delivered 14.5 percent annual gains over the past decade.

Two similar funds, Mutual Beacon and Mutual Qualified, for tax-deferred retirement accounts, have provided even better returns during that time. The kicker: the funds have been only about half as volatile as the typical equity fund.

In 1993, Price launched Mutual Discovery, which buys smaller company stocks. It has gained roughly 19 percent annually during the past three years and has been about 40 percent as volatile as the typical small company stock fund.
A new fund, Mutual European, has generated high expectations among fund trackers, who point out that many of Price's best picks in recent years have come from abroad.

The funds' records reflect Price's almost-unique investment style, which calls for an eclectic mix of securities. About half of each fund's portfolio is devoted to conventional "value" stocks. They include shares of companies that have delivered disappointing earnings or suffered other setbacks, causing their shares to decline to prices that do not reflect their true long-term potential.

Price also invests a slug of the portfolios in "deal" stocks -- shares of companies involved in mergers, reorganizations, bankruptcies and other transactions. His mentor Max Heine was an early investor in securities of bankrupt companies, fishing out value in corners that didn't interest most analysts.

While such securities can be risky, they typically don't move in concert with the overall stock market. Thus, they tend to hold up better than most stocks in a broad market downturn. Moreover, Price typically holds 10 percent to 20 percent of the portfolios in cash. Apart from its value as a hedge against market declines, the cash gives Price the freedom to snap up bargains whenever they occur.

Some analysts are worried that Price won't be able to maintain the funds' performances once Franklin's vaunted sales force starts selling their shares. Right now, the largest fund, Mutual Shares, has assets of $6.2 billion -- not enormous by today's standards. But it's likely that the funds will grow quickly, making it harder to find the kinds of bargains that have made them stellar performers in the past.

Price responds that he has hired more people and will have little trouble finding opportunities in this country and abroad. And he could be right. One reason: very few funds or investment managers do what he does. Rather than snoop around for bargain-priced stocks or obscure securities issued by bankrupt companies, today's fund managers prefer to invest in the hottest sectors of the moment, such as technology stocks.
As a result, the Mutual Series funds look like good bets to deliver solid gains at modest risk for a long time to come.

That said, some fund investors can't bring themselves to pay a sales commission. They might want to consider another value-oriented fund with a similar investment approach, such as the Third Avenue Value Fund (800-443-1021; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load).

Like Price, Third Avenue Value manager Marty Whitman is one of the most highly regarded mutual fund managers around. Also like Price, he finds value in corners of the market that other investors ignore or don't understand. For example, Whitman recently invested in the debt of financially troubled Kmart, which he believes will be an attractive investment even if the company's financial woes continue.

The fund's 16.2 percent average annual return during the past five years is almost as good as Price's funds. What's more, Whitman buys extremely cheap stocks and bonds, which has kept the fund only about 60 percent as volatile as the average growth fund tracked by Morningstar Mutual Funds in Chicago.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
